#10399. Securing FastAPI Applications: JWT Authentication and Rate Limiting with Redis

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Building a modern web API is only half the battle. Ensuring it is secure, resilient, and capable of handling malicious traffic is what separates a hobby project from a production-ready service. When building highly scalable applications, we typically lean on stateless architectures. However, features like token revocation and rate limiting require state.

In this guide, we will explore the architectural concepts behind building a secure API using FastAPI, Redis, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), and SlowAPI. We will break down the theory, the tech stack, and the flow of data—without getting bogged down in the code.

Before diving into the architecture, it is crucial to understand the role each tool plays in our security model:

Security starts with how you manage your secrets. The first step in our architectural journey is setting up a configuration file and a local environment file.

Hardcoding secret keys, database URLs, or algorithm types directly into your application is a severe security risk. Instead, we load these from environment variables. The application uses a settings manager to read variables like the Redis host, port, the JWT secret key, the algorithm (typically HS256), and the token expiration time. This ensures that sensitive data stays out of your version control system.

To handle rate limiting and token tracking, we need a connection to Redis. Because FastAPI is inherently asynchronous, we initialize an asynchronous Redis client.

Redis acts as the central state-holder for our API. By using Redis, we ensure that even if our API is running on five different servers behind a load balancer, the rate limits and the token blacklists remain globally synchronized.

Next, we establish the utility functions that handle the cryptographic heavy lifting. This step is divided into two main parts:

Here, we initialize the FastAPI application and attach slowapi.

slowapi needs a way to identify the client making the request. By default, it uses the client's IP address. We attach the limiter to the application state and register an exception handler. This ensures that if a user breaches the rate limit, the API gracefully returns a "429 Too Many Requests" error instead of crashing.

We also set up a dependency that acts as a security guard for our protected routes. This dependency intercepts incoming requests, extracts the token, and decodes it. It then checks Redis to see if the token has been blacklisted (for example, if the user logged out before the token expired). If the token is valid and not blacklisted, the request proceeds; otherwise, a "401 Unauthorized" error is thrown.

The login endpoint is where the magic happens. When a user submits their credentials, the API verifies the username and password. In a production scenario, this involves querying a database; in our example, we verify it against a hardcoded credential.

Once the credentials are validated, the API generates a JWT. To ensure we can invalidate this token later if needed, we store the token in Redis with a time-to-live (TTL) that matches the token's expiration time. Finally, the token is returned to the client, which will store it and send it in the Authorization header of future requests.

Finally, we create a route that requires both authentication and rate limiting.

Before the route's logic even executes, two things happen:

If the client passes both security checks, they are granted access to the highly secure data provided by the route.

To validate this system, you would conceptually walk through several test scenarios. First, you test the login flow with correct and incorrect credentials to ensure tokens are only issued to valid users.

Next, you test the rate limit by rapidly firing requests at the protected route to ensure the "429 Too Many Requests" response triggers. Finally, you test the security guard by trying to access the route with no token, an expired token, and a manually blacklisted token to ensure the API correctly denies access in all scenarios.

Building a secure API requires layering defenses. By combining FastAPI's speed, Redis's fast state management, JWT's stateless authentication, and slowapi's rate-limiting capabilities, you create a system that is both robust and scalable.

While this foundational text explains the core concepts, moving to production requires adding token refresh flows, implementing per-user rate limiting (rather than just IP-based), deploying Redis with high availability, and ensuring your secrets are managed by a secure vault. These practices will ensure your API remains secure as your user base grows.

Mesh routers are among the hottest-selling types of routers in networking, and leading the charge are products based on the Wi-Fi 7 standard. Mesh routers enable you to fully cover your home or office with wireless coverage that would otherwise be impossible with a single, standalone router.

Fortunately, numerous manufacturers are producing Wi-Fi 7 mesh routers, offering a wide range of options to choose from. If you prefer seamless integration with your Amazon account and Alexa services, consider opting for the Eero Pro 7. If you want endless configuration options and no-cost features, such as extensive Parental Controls, the Asus ZenWiFi BT4 has you covered. If you're looking for a delicate balance of performance and features at a bargain price, consider the TP-Link Deco BE95.

However, one thing to keep in mind when shopping for a network upgrade is that not all Wi-Fi 7 routers are created equal. While there are speed differences between products that depend on several factors (channel width, total number of streams, etc.), the primary differentiator among Wi-Fi 7 routers comes down to the number of supported bands. There are dual- and tri-band routers, with the latter offering the best potential performance. Dual-band routers only support the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands, while tri-band routers support the higher-performing and shorter-range 6 GHz band. The maximum performance of the 6 GHz band is what gives tri-band Wi-Fi 7 routers a significant theoretical speed advantage over their Wi-Fi 6E predecessors.

Some manufacturers, such as Asus, also offer quad-band routers that feature either two 5 GHz wireless bands or two 6 GHz bands.

With that said, check out the extensive list below for all the best deals on Wi-Fi 7 routers from Asus, Eero, Netgear, MSI, and TP-Link.

The Asus ZenWiFi BD4 is an entry-level Wi-Fi 7 router and thus only supports two bands (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz). This 3-pack features up to 3.6 Gbps of combined throughput and covers 6,500 square feet.

The Deco BE23 is TP-Link's most entry-level Wi-Fi 7 router, sporting dual-band wireless, up to 3.6 Gbps throughput, and coverage of 4,500 square feet.

The Deco BE63 is a mid-range, tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router with four 2.5 GbE ports, 10 Gbps of combined throughput, and coverage of 5,800 square feet.

The TP-Link Deco 7 Pro BE10000 is a tri-band, Wi-Fi 7 mesh system that includes three wireless nodes. Each node comes with four 2.5 GbE ports, and the total wireless coverage is 7,600 square feet.

TP-Link's flagship Deco BE95 Wi-Fi 7 mesh router supports four bands, delivering up to 33 Gbps of throughput. It also features two 10 GbE ports per node.

The Eero Pro 7 is a mid-range, tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router that offers coverage of up to 4,000 square feet. Each wireless node features two 5 GbE ports.

The Eero Max 7 is Amazon's flagship Wi-Fi 7 router, featuring tri-band wireless, two 2.5 GbE ports, two 10 GbE ports, and up to 5,000 square feet of coverage.

The Orbi 770 is the latest in Netgear's long line of Orbi mesh routers. This one is a tri-band system with coverage of up to 5,500 square feet and 11 Gbps of combined throughput. You also get three 2.5 GbE ports and one 2.5 GbE port for WAN.

MSI's Roamii BE Lite is a newcomer on the Wi-Fi 7 mesh router scene, and it's a dual-band unit. Each node includes 2.5 GbE ports, and MSI even provides wall mounts in the box.

The MSI Roamii BE Pro is a high-powered, tri-band Wi-Fi 7 mesh router that won't break the bank. Each node includes four 2.5 GbE ports for connecting your wired devices, and the mesh system is controlled by a rather feature-packed smartphone app.

If you want a high-performance mesh router, look no further. The Asus ZenWiFi BE30000 is a quad-band solution, featuring three wireless nodes. Aggregate speeds across all four bands (you get two 6 GHz bands, one of which is dedicated to a wireless backhaul) are 30 Gbps, and you get coverage for up to 11,000 square feet.

#10393. How AI Image-to-Image and Image-to-Video Tools Work, and How to Build a Reliable Workflow

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Creating polished visual content used to require professional equipment, editing skills and hours of manual work. Generative AI has changed that for photographers, designers, marketers and developers who build creative tools, but the results depend heavily on understanding what these systems actually do. Two techniques sit at the center of most workflows: image-to-image generation, which transforms an existing picture, and image-to-video generation, which adds motion to a still.

This article explains how both techniques work, which settings control the outcome, how several kinds of tools differ, and how to assemble a workflow with review steps, including a short code example you can run yourself. It also covers rights, authenticity and the limits of the technology. Feature details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing and change often, so confirm current terms before you plan a production.

Image-to-image resembles text-to-image, but it starts from your picture instead of pure noise. According to the Hugging Face Diffusers image-to-image guide, the initial image is encoded into latent space and noise is added to it. The model then uses the prompt and the noisy latent to predict and remove that noise, and a decoder converts the result back into an image.

A single setting, usually called strength or creativity, decides how much of the original remains. In Diffusers, a higher strength gives the model more freedom, and a value of 1.0 means the starting image is largely ignored. Strength is linked to the number of denoising steps: with 50 inference steps and a strength of 0.8, the pipeline adds noise for 40 steps and then denoises for 40.

The ranges above are rules of thumb, not guarantees. Models and tools respond differently, so test on your own images. The script below, adapted from the Diffusers documentation, sweeps four strength values on one source image so you can compare them side by side.

Running this requires a compatible GPU setup and model downloads, and the checkpoint name and defaults can change between library versions, so check the current documentation.

Plain image-to-image can drift from the layout you wanted. Research such as ControlNet adds spatial control to pretrained text-to-image diffusion models, with conditions such as edges, depth, segmentation and human pose. In practice, this is why many tools offer reference images, sketches, masks and pose guides on top of a prompt: they supply structure that a text prompt cannot describe precisely.

The key advantage is speed of iteration. The main limits are consistency between variations, small details such as hands and text, and the gap between a convincing concept and a usable final asset.

The right tool depends on what you need to control and where the output will be used. The table summarizes what each vendor’s own page states, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

OpenArt’s own page describes an AI image to image generator that accepts JPEG, PNG, WEBP or HEIC files, offers a creativity slider and an optional reference image, and lets you switch between several models. Its FAQ advises uploading only images you own or have rights to use. Adobe’s Firefly page describes generative editing and video tools and states that outputs include Content Credentials, while saying its own models were trained on licensed and public-domain content. These are vendor statements, so read the current terms for the plan you use.

Image-to-video uses a still as the starting point for an animated scene. Most current systems extend diffusion models across time, so that a whole sequence of frames is denoised together. The research paper Video Diffusion Models describes this extension from images to video. The practical consequence is that the first frame strongly shapes what follows, so a clean composition and a clear subject make better clips.

For example, a still of a person walking through a rainy city can be animated with falling rain, reflections and a slow camera move. The motion instruction should describe one clear action and one camera movement rather than a long list.

Kling’s main site announces Kling 4.0 and describes stable dynamic motion with an audio-visual experience, with image-to-video features and an API platform listed. OpenArt’s Kling 4.0 page describes how the model is offered on that platform. According to that page, videos run from 3 to 30 seconds at 720p to 1080p, you can use up to 10 keyframes and up to 15 references, and you can save a character for reuse. The page does not state pricing or generation quotas for the model. Capabilities depend on the platform that provides access and on the settings available there, so check supported inputs, output limits and cost before planning a production.

Generated motion needs checking. Warped limbs, drifting faces, flickering textures and unwanted text are common. A quick review script samples frames and reports basic file properties:

Consider a small business preparing a campaign for a new skincare product. The same steps apply to any visual project.

This process reduces the effort of exploring concepts and makes it easier to test several versions of an advertisement before choosing a direction. It does not remove the need for human review.

They can be, with different priorities. Photographers can explore creative treatments, mood boards and alternative backgrounds without replacing traditional photography. Marketers can develop campaign concepts, create variations of social graphics and test promotional videos. In both cases the value comes from supporting a clear creative objective rather than adopting a tool because it is new.

A technique that transforms an existing image using a prompt, by adding noise to the image and then regenerating it under guidance. A strength or creativity setting controls how much of the original is kept.

Use a lower strength, a reference image or a structure condition such as edges or depth where the tool supports it.

Yes. Image-to-video tools animate a still from a motion description, though complex motion can introduce inconsistencies, so review every clip.

No. Several vendors and platforms offer video generation. Compare supported inputs, length, resolution, cost and licensing against your needs.

It depends on the tool, the plan and the rights you hold in the inputs. Read the current terms and keep records of your sources.

Image-to-image and image-to-video tools give creators a faster way to explore ideas, but they work best when you understand their controls. Strength settings decide how much of the original survives, conditioning methods preserve structure, and the starting frame shapes video. Compare hosted platforms, vendor apps and open-source libraries against your needs, build review and provenance into the workflow, and treat the output as a draft that a person checks before it ships.

#10389. Microsoft is shutting down the ‘To Do’ app that replaced Wunderlist, with no real replacement

Microsoft announced this week that its To Do app is shutting down soon, taking the legacy of Wunderlist with it.

Microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app. The company explains:

As we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do. The To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027. Connections that other apps use to access To Do tasks will continue beyond that date, and we’ll provide separate notice before those connections are retired. We’re also updating existing task integrations across Microsoft 365 to connect with Planner, so you’ll be able to create or manage tasks in the Microsoft experiences you already use. Although To Do tasks are already visible in Planner, they will not be migrated to the new private plan. Customers using personal Microsoft accounts will need to choose another app. Our To Do transition guidance  will help you understand what’s changing and plan your next steps.

To Do was built on the foundation of Wunderlist, a wildly popular to do list app that Microsoft purchased in 2015. Wunderlist later shut down in 2020.

Microsoft’s shuffle, notably, leaves general consumers without a replacement app. To Do was available to anyone with a Microsoft account, where Planner is available only to enterprise/business users. So, for long-time Wunderlist users who followed Microsoft migration, this is the end of the road and it’s officially time to move to another app.

As you can see from the data from our GPU benchmark hierarchy, the RTX 5060 is a graphics card that's most comfortable at 1080p, though it can scale up to 1440p, assuming you're willing to lean into Nvidia's DLSS suite between Super Resolution and Multi-Frame Generation, both of which are supported on this GPU.

Its main limitation is the 8GB frame buffer, which could pose issues in some titles at 1440p. For the vast majority of 1080p games, it shouldn't be a problem. In our testing of DLSS 5, which is supported on the RTX 5060, we found that the 8GB frame buffer posed a limitation on performance. However, Nvidia has already apparently slashed the VRAM usage of its DLSS 5 model. The RTX 5060 was fast enough to reach 58 FPS at 1080p with DLSS 5 still.

Outside of the GPU, the Core i5-14400F is the perfect CPU for a rig like this. It provides performance on the level of the Core i5-14600K in games while sacrificing a bit of peak productivity power and the unlocked multiplier.

The one major downside with this configuration is the single 16GB DDR4-3200 DIMM. With just a single stick, your bandwidth is cut in half. Thankfully, the motherboard has four DIMM slots, so you can add another 16GB module to double your capacity and unlock the full bandwidth. Thankfully, DDR4 is much cheaper than DDR5, as you can see in our RAM price tracker.

#10384. Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

Long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models. Longer native sequence lengths give large language models (LLMs) the working memory to read a whole code repository or ingest hours of video, and reason through multi-step agentic tasks. In three years, context windows have grown from 128K–200K tokens to 1M–2M, and models trained toward 10M tokens are arriving. Training at those lengths, not just serving them, is where the system limits show up.

In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:

Today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework. MaxText enables this by supporting four context-parallel strategies on Cloud TPU: All-gather, A2A (DeepSpeed Ulysses), P2P (Ring Attention), and the A2A + P2P hybrid (Unified Sequence Parallelism, or USP), combined with load balancing and sequence packing. All four use the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel. Combined with the 3D inter-chip interconnect (ICI) ( supported on TPUs such as TPU 5p or TPU 7 (Ironwood) ), this lets one sequence span an entire slice while communication overlaps compute and memory per chip stays flat. In our benchmarks, Llama 3.1 8B (25 head dim, 16 query heads) demonstrates exceptional long-context efficiency, achieving 70% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) on TPU 5p for sequence lengths up to 4 million tokens. Across both TPU 5p and TPU 7, context can be seamlessly extended to 14 million tokens—with TPU 7 consistently maintaining 50% MFU across all sequence scales below 6 million tokens.

This functionality is available today in MaxText v0.2.4(doc).

Context parallelism splits a long sequence across chips, so no chip holds the activations of the whole sequence. Context parallelism can be combined with data and tensor parallelism, and the smallest context-parallel size that fits your sequence in HBM is usually the right one. This also holds for sparser attention variants which cut attention compute but not the activations of every other layer.

Attention is the one global operation where every token needs the keys and values of every preceding token, so each context parallel strategy has to bring those keys and values back together. Each makes a different tradeoff between memory (how much KV a chip holds), communication (how much moves per layer, and whether it overlaps compute), and model shape (how many attention heads to split).

All-gather: Each chip keeps its chunk of the sequence and, at every layer, gathers the keys and values from every other chip. It is the simplest option. However, because causal masking causes later tokens to attend to larger prefixes, All-gather requires balancing compute load across devices.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

All-to-All (Ulysses): Gathering keys and values makes every chip hold the whole sequence, so attention memory never shrinks no matter how many chips you add. All-to-All changes what each chip owns instead. Attention is independent across heads but not across tokens, so the head axis is free to shard and the token axis is not. An All-to-All before attention rotates the sharding from one onto the other: each chip gives up the heads it is not responsible for and receives the tokens it was missing for the heads it keeps, ending up with the full sequence for a few heads instead of a few tokens for all heads. This is also why Ulysses does not need token load balancing. Attention then runs as ordinary single-chip attention with standard kernels, and a second All-to-All rotates the output back. KV per chip shrinks by the context-parallel factor, but you cannot split across more chips than the model has heads — and tensor parallelism shards that same dimension, so TP × CP is capped by the head count (under GQA, by the KV heads: eight for Llama 3 8B). The all-to-all itself, though, does not overlap with compute — attention cannot start on a partial sequence, so every chip waits for data from every other chip before any of them begins.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

P2P (ring attention): Ulysses' ceiling is the head count; ring attention removes it by never leaving the token axis. Keys and values never materialize in full. KV chunks travel around a ring of chips one hop at a time, neighbor to neighbor. Each chip attends its queries to the chunk it holds while the next one is in flight, and merges the partial results as it goes. A chip holds its own chunk and one visiting chunk, never the full sequence, and the communication overlaps compute. However, dividing attention computation into smaller chunks can reduce local kernel efficiency, and unlike All-to-All Ulysses, ring attention requires explicit load balancing.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

A2A + P2P (USP): A2A + P2P (USP): Neither strategy scales on its own — All-to-All stops at the head count, and a long ring accumulates hops while thinning the overlap that makes it work. Unified sequence parallelism composes them on two axes of the chip mesh, so the context-parallel degree becomes the product of the two: All-to-All along one axis, sized at or below the KV-head count, and a ring along the other to extend past it. Because each All-to-All group has already pooled its tokens, a ring step now carries a chunk larger by the All-to-All factor, and the ring is correspondingly shorter — more compute per hop to hide the transfer behind, and fewer hops to accumulate latency and causal imbalance. On Cloud TPU the two map onto two axes of the slice's chip mesh.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

These strategies cover the attention variants in today's major models, from multi-head and grouped-query attention to DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention.

Splitting the sequence only pays off if the attention compute on each chip stays efficient. All four strategies run on Splash Attention, the block-sparse flash attention kernel from Tokamax, Google's open-source library of TPU kernels. It skips fully masked blocks and handles packed sequences without padding. P2P calls it once per ring step, on the local queries and the KV chunk that has just arrived, while the transfer for the next step runs underneath, in the forward and backward pass alike. Each chip does the same fused, block-level work it would do without context parallelism, with the communication hidden behind it.

P2P (Ring Attention) is the primary workhorse for very long-context training, whereas All-Gather is the standard baseline for most other cases where the KV can fit. These are the primary CP strategies to use in practice. We compare how far each can push context length on a fixed 64-chip TPU 5p slice with Llama 3.1 8B (256 head dim, 16 query heads) , and measure their MFUs. In ideal settings where both strategies can have large enough chunks (S/CP) and local batch size - the two major variables driving MFU on TPU 5p, we observe that P2P can outperform All-Gather almost every context length from 64K to 14M tokens, where communication becomes mostly hidden with the Ring circular transport schedule.

TPU v7x (Ironwood) takes the same recipe further. With twice the HBM per chip, P2P training of 14M tokens on 64 TPU 7 chips reached 48.7% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) compared to 37.1% on TPU 5p. We observed that ring attention performs better than other context parallelism strategies -- e.g. Ulysses and USP –- on TPU 7 chips.

The choice of context parallelism strategy depends mostly on whether the gathered KV fits in HBM, and on how many KV heads the model has:

For all CP strategies, when you run low on memory: Offload before you recompute. MaxText can move saved activations, optimizer states, and parameters to host memory tensor by tensor. At long context lengths, these transfers are hidden behind compute, making offloading effectively free. Offload attention outputs first, followed by optimizer states, layer inputs, parameters, and finally remat as a last resort. MFU stays flat through the offload steps while all-gather falls off and eventually stops fitting. For more details, see the remat tuning guide.

Looking ahead, we see two natural extensions. The first is broader model coverage. Models that mix sliding-window and global layers, such as Gemma, would run the window layers with a short exchange between neighboring chips while the global layers use the ring. We also plan to support linear attention mechanisms such as Gated Delta Net (GDN) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). The second is performance, with further tuning of the Tokamax kernels and the P2P backward pass to narrow the remaining gap to all-gather at short context, and recipes by model and context length for TPU 5p and 7 chips.

Context parallelism is available today in MaxText v0.2.4 on PyPI, the corresponding Docker images and on GitHub main. Sample recipes are available here for TPU 7 and TPU 5p. Pick a strategy with context_parallel_strategy (ring, ulysses, or usp), set the context-parallel size, and keep the rest of your run the same. The sharding guide has the flags and constraints for each strategy, and the release notes link to the pull requests behind this work. We can't wait to see what you train.

#10382. Expect Samsung’s good-value Galaxy devices to get more expensive, report says

Rising memory costs are hitting mid-range devices the hardest. The latest report suggests Samsung will increase the price of its Galaxy A device series by 19% next year.

The report comes from Korean news outlet SEDaily. An industry source has reportedly stated that Samsung plans to increase the price of its mid-range phones starting next year. More specifically, the Galaxy A series.

The range between price jumps varies across a reported 8 Galaxy A series devices, but the highest value difference nearly hits a notable 19% increase. The largest jump reaches 18.6% for the Galaxy A17, which could increase from $269 to $319. It would no longer sit in a sub-$300 spot and wouldn’t be much of a value buy anymore.

Again, these are phones praised for sitting at a convenient price point. Samsung’s Galaxy A devices are generally good value and offer a lot of the best One UI features for a price that doesn’t come close to the current flagship selling points.

This comes after a report came out last month indicating Samsung cut production of its Galaxy A devices by “approximately 20%.” Memory makes up more of the overall component cost in mid-range devices. So the cost of the overall device is more influenced by memory prices than in a flagship, like the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Even with a specced-out build, there’s more dispersion of costly components, rather than one expensive component like memory taking up the bulk of the production price.

That cut is estimated to be around 10 million units, and this latest report only furthers the claim that mid-range devices are too costly to make for Samsung.

The opposite is true for the Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, which reportedly got the green light for increased production prior to launch. Price suggestions average an increase of $200 for the Galaxy S27 and Galaxy S27 Plus. As for the high-spec Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, they start at $1,399 and $1,499, respectively.

There was already a massive disparity between those devices and the increasingly validated Galaxy A devices, and the gap is shrinking.

Converting Markdown to PDF is easy until the document has real content: long code blocks, wide tables, images and non-Latin text are where most tools fall apart.

Pandoc with LaTeX is still the most powerful route, but it needs a large install and trips over Unicode and emoji unless you switch engines and fonts.

Browser-based approaches (print CSS, Chromium-powered converters, in-browser tools) avoid the install and give you HTML-quality rendering, as long as you control page breaks.

A handful of print CSS rules (@page, break-inside: avoid, break-after: avoid) fix the majority of ugly PDFs, whichever tool you use.

Choose the tool by the document: a quick README export, a long technical report and a multilingual document each have a different best option.

I write almost everything in Markdown: READMEs, release notes, client handovers, meeting notes. And at least once a week, someone asks for "the PDF version". Every time, the conversion looks fine on the first page and falls apart somewhere around page three: a code block split in half, a table running off the edge, an emoji replaced by an empty box.

SitePoint covered the classic route back in 2015 with Creating PDFs from Markdown with Pandoc and LaTeX. That approach still works. But a lot has changed since then, and today there are several ways to get a clean PDF without installing a TeX distribution. This article compares them, then goes through the rendering problems you'll actually hit, with a fix for each.

Pandoc is still the Swiss Army knife. The simplest command is:

By default, that goes through LaTeX, which means you need a TeX distribution installed (several gigabytes for a full one). The output is beautiful for prose and math, but LaTeX has strong opinions about layout, and customizing it means writing LaTeX.

Pandoc can also render through an HTML engine instead, which lets you style the PDF with CSS:

Best for: long documents, academic writing, math, automated pipelines.

Watch out for: install size, Unicode handling with the default engine (more on that below).

Render the Markdown to HTML (any previewer, a static site, a GitHub page) and print it to PDF. It's free and already installed everywhere, but you inherit whatever the page looks like on screen: navigation bars, sidebars, and page breaks wherever they happen to fall.

Best for: quick, one-off exports of short documents.

Watch out for: zero control over page breaks unless the page ships print CSS.

Extensions like Markdown PDF for VS Code, or CLI tools like md-to-pdf, render your Markdown to HTML and print it with a headless Chromium:

You get the same rendering quality as a browser, plus a config file for CSS, margins, headers and footers. The trade-off is a Node install and a downloaded Chromium.

Best for: developers who live in their editor or want CI-friendly exports.

Watch out for: the first run downloads a browser, and print CSS is still your job.

The newest option is tools that do the whole conversion inside the browser tab: you paste or drop the .md file, preview the actual pages and download the PDF. The good ones don't upload your file anywhere, which matters for client documents and internal notes.

Best for: people who don't want to install anything, non-developers on your team, private documents.

Watch out for: many online converters do upload your file to a server; check before you paste anything confidential.

Whichever method you pick, the same handful of problems show up as soon as the document is longer than a page. Most of them are fixed with print CSS, which works in Pandoc's HTML engines, Chromium-based tools and any HTML you print from a browser.

A 20-line function cut after line 3, with the rest on the next page, is the most common complaint. The fix is to ask the renderer not to break inside the block:

One caveat: a block longer than a full page has to break. For those, it's better to let it break cleanly than to push it to a new page and leave a huge gap.

On screen, a long line in a code block scrolls horizontally. On paper, there's no scrollbar, so it's simply cut off. Wrap long lines in print:

Tables with many columns overflow the page or get squeezed until every cell is one word per line. Three things help: a smaller font size for tables, a landscape page for the worst offenders, and avoiding breaks in the middle of short tables:

If a table genuinely needs eight columns, consider whether it should be a table in the PDF at all, or an appendix in landscape.

A heading alone at the bottom of a page, with its content on the next one, looks broken. This rule keeps a heading attached to what follows it:

Support for break-after: avoid varies between rendering engines, so test it with yours; when it isn't honored, a manual page break before the heading is the reliable fallback.

Markdown has no syntax for a page break. The usual trick is a raw HTML element that print CSS turns into a break:

Some converters also recognize a comment like , which has the advantage of staying invisible when the same file is rendered on GitHub.

Images are inserted at their natural size, so a 4000-pixel screenshot spills off the page. Cap them:

For blurry images, the problem is usually the opposite: a small screenshot stretched to page width. Export screenshots at 2x if they're going into a PDF.

This one is specific to the LaTeX route. With the default pdflatex engine, Unicode characters outside its supported set produce errors or simply vanish. Switch to XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX and give it a font that actually contains the characters:

Emoji are harder still in LaTeX and often need a dedicated package. HTML-based renderers handle both far better, because they use the operating system's font fallback just like a web page does.

Internal links ([see setup](#setup)) and external links should stay clickable. HTML-based renderers usually keep both. If yours doesn't, check that headings get IDs (most Markdown parsers add them) and that the PDF engine preserves link annotations.

Put together, these rules make a solid starting point for any HTML-based route:

Save it as print.css and pass it to Pandoc (--css=print.css with an HTML engine), to md-to-pdf through its config, or include it in the HTML you print from the browser.

My rule of thumb after a lot of trial and error:

A quick README or notes export, no install, private content: an in-browser converter. Full disclosure: this need is why I built the free Markdown to PDF converter on AwesomeToolkit, and it's what I use for this case now. It renders real A4 or Letter pages as you type, has an option to keep code blocks and tables whole, adds page numbers and a table of contents, and the conversion happens in the browser, so the file isn't uploaded anywhere.

Documentation in a repo, exported in CI: md-to-pdf or Pandoc with an HTML engine, plus the stylesheet above.

Long reports, math, academic formatting: Pandoc with XeLaTeX, using a font that covers every script in the document.

Something you'll print once and forget: the browser's Print to PDF is fine.

Whatever you choose, the biggest quality jump comes from the print rules, not the tool. Ten lines of CSS turn "it looks fine until page three" into a PDF you can actually send.

Yes. Your browser's Print to PDF works on any rendered Markdown, and in-browser converters do the whole conversion in a tab. Check that the converter processes files locally if the content is private.

The default pdflatex engine has limited Unicode support. Use --pdf-engine=xelatex or lualatex and set a font that contains the characters with -V mainfont= (and -V CJKmainfont= for CJK text).

Markdown has no native syntax for it. Insert

where you want the break, or use the page-break comment your converter supports.

Add pre { break-inside: avoid; } to your print CSS. Blocks longer than a page will still break, which is expected.

With HTML-based renderers, usually yes, both external links and links to headings inside the document. Test internal links in particular, since they depend on headings having IDs.

These give you a lightening-fast response time with a 0.1mm press sensitivity, along with adjustable actuation points for per-key customization. This gives you full flexibility over the entire board.

You've got two options on sale, with the all-black and all-white options at the same $115.99 price: a great deal on a full-size Hall effect keyboard. — Ben Stockton

Anker has carved a name for itself in the portable power bank business, and it's a familiar option for Amazon buyers. Right now, you can pick up its laptop power bank, with a huge 25,000 mAh battery capacity, for just $91.19. That's a 32% discount compared to its usual list price.

The Anker Laptop Power Bank can supply up to 165 watts when two USB-C ports are in use. It also features a retractable USB-C cable and another integrated cable that doubles as a carrying strap.

$91 is enough to get you a power bank with three USB-C ports, including one retractable cable, each capable of 100W each, with a USB-A port capable of 33W. If you're using more than one USB-C cable, you can output a maximum of 165W between them or 133W if you’re using one USB-C port and the USB-A port. If you max out the power bank by using all four ports simultaneously, you’re limited to 130 watts maximum output.

This will let you power up a smartphone, laptop, portable game console, and more, with up to 100W each to supported devices. If your laptop can push that far, it'll carry on charging your laptop until it depletes. It's also capable of charging up itself with a 100W-charger, gaining 30% in 22 minutes.

There's also a built-in display that lets you see charge, device temperature and battery health. If you're on-the-go with plenty of devices in your bag, this is the kind of battery pack you'll want at your disposal. — Ben Stockton

Our favorite gaming chair isn't a typical racing-style chair, but it's not an office one, either. It's this collab between Herman Miller and Logitech G. The Vantum, ergonomic but "built for gamers" with gaming features like an adjustable neckrest, lumbar support and forward-leaning alignment is on sale right now for $768.07 right now, down from $1,155, with an extra 5% off thanks to a Black Friday promo code.

Features an "active, forward leaning alignment," adjustable lumbar support, and passively-adaptive thoracic support. It has a foam-padded seat cushion and a mesh suspension backrest for breathability, as well as an adjustable neck rest.

The Vantum is a seriously premium chair. It has a mesh backrest and a padded cushioned seat, along with 4D armrests with padding. As you can imagine, it scored well in our Herman Miller x Logitech G Vantum review, thanks to its lightweight but comfortable design, with the adjustable lumbar support similar to the functionality you'd see in the company's pricier Herman Miller task chairs.

While the chair doesn't offer full recline, its tilt mechanism is pretty comfortable, as is the passively-adaptive thoracic support. This Black Friday discount means you can save $386.93, as long as you use the SAVE5 code at checkout to get the full discount. — Ben Stockton

The Logitech Yeti Orb is the spiritual successor to the classic Blue Snowball microphone — it's a unique-looking, ball-shaped microphone that sits on top of a sturdy desktop tripod stand and sounds great out of the box. It's our favorite budget-priced gaming mic and it's on sale right now for an even more budget-friendly $39.99 at Best Buy — $30 off its MSRP of $69.99.

This round, ball-shaped desktop mic features a cardioid polar pattern and sounds great out of the box. It comes with a desktop stand and has customizable RGB lighting, and can be mounted at two different angles.

The Yeti Orb is a simple, stylish microphone that comes with a plastic desktop tripod stand in the box. It has the Blue Snowball's iconic ball shape, with two mounting points — so you can mount it straight on, or at an angle, depending on whether you're mounting it on the included stand or on a boom arm. There are no on-mic controls or ports (other than its USB-C port), so you won't be able to adjust the mic's gain or plug in a headset for zero-latency monitoring, and for that reason it's not really a mic for serious streamers. But it does have customizable RGB lighting, which indicates whether the mic is recording, and it sounds great right out of the box — so while you can tweak the settings using Logitech G Hub (which comes with Blue Vo!ce), you don't have to. It's a great mic for casual chatting and streaming, and this is a great price to get it at. You can read my full review of the Logitech Yeti Orb here. — Sarah

Corsair's wireless MMO / MOBA-focused gaming mouse features 16 programmable buttons, including 12 in a side array, and sports Corsair's 33K Marksman S optical sensor. It also has native integration with Elgato's Stream Deck platform, so you can map Stream Deck commands directly to the buttons.

If you're looking for a mouse with tons of buttons, look no further than Corsair's Scimitar line — the Corsair Scimitar Elite SE Wireless is currently on sale for just $69.99 at Best Buy, which is 50% off its retail price of $139.99. And if you don't need a wireless mouse, the wired Corsair Scimitar RGB Elite is down to $49.99 at Amazon, which is 44% off its retail price of $89.99.

The Scimitar RGB Elite mouse from Corsair features 17 programmable buttons, including 12 located on the side panel, the left/right primary mouse buttons, two DPI switch buttons above the scroll wheel, and the scroll wheel's center click. You can slide the 12-button side panel to fit your hand size.

The Corsair Scimitar Elite SE Wireless is an MMO / MOBA-focused gaming mouse with an adjustable 12-button side panel — it doesn't swap out, like the side panel on the Razer Naga V2 / V3 Pro, but it does move forward and back (it comes with a hex tool so you can adjust it to where you want and lock it in). It doesn't move a ton, but it's a nice accommodation for people who find that the giant gaming mice that dominate the market don't have buttons in quite the right places.

The Scimitar Elite SE Wireless sports Corsair's Marksman S 33K sensor, which has a maximum resolution of 33,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 750 IPS and can handle up to 50 G's of force. It's a heavier mouse — 4.02oz / 114g, but weight isn't that big of a deal in the MMO / MOBA community. Also, it's integrated with Elgato's Stream Deck platform, so you can program Stream Deck functionality directly to the mouse's buttons. You can read my full review of the Corsair Scimitar Elite SE Wireless here. — Sarah

The 9800X3D might not be the fastest gaming CPU on the market but it's still the best option owing to its speed and power draw. Now, at Amazon, it just crashed to an all-time low of $369, thanks to a coupon you can apply before checking out.

The Ryzen 7 9800X3D is a potent gaming 8-core, 16-thread desktop CPU. It has a massive 96MB L3 cache for gaming performance, with clock speeds of up to 5.2GHz.

The 9800X3D really needs no introduction, but in case you aren't familiar, this is one the best gaming CPUs around. IT isn't quite AMD's fastest — the 9850X3D takes that crown — but this chip draws significantly less power while still being very close in terms of performance. The industry leading 3D V-Cache means the CPU is much less reliant on your slower RAM, drastically boosting frame rates.

This deal is not likely to be around for long, so move fast if you want one to start an AM5 build or upgrade your existing rig. - Stephen Warwick

This TKL mechanical keyboard features hot-swappable switches and a built-in Stream Deck with 12 LCD keys, a 2.75-inch screen, and 2 rotary knobs.

The Corsair Galleon 100 SD is a keyboard with an integrated Stream Deck — it's a mechanical keyboard with a TKL layout, plus a 2-knob, 12-key Stream Deck that has all the functionality of Elgato's Stream Deck platform. Although I still lament the lack of a true 10-key numberpad, I have to admit that the Corsair Galleon 100 SD has been my daily driver for the better part of the past year. Who knew an integrated Stream Deck was so useful?!

Of course, at $350... it's definitely not cheap. But right now it's down to $259.99 at Best Buy — $90 off its retail price, and a pretty good deal when you consider you're getting both a keyboard and a Stream Deck in one.

The Galleon 100 SD is a pretty premium keyboard, with a nice-looking design, double-shot PBT keycaps, a pass-through USB port, and a hot-swappable PCB. It comes with only one switch option: Corsair's MLX Pulse (purple) switches, which are "thocky and linear" — and they sound pretty good, though they're definitely linear. The case has six layers of sound-dampening foam and it's a great-sounding keyboard overall, especially for a mainstream gaming keyboard.

The Stream Deck features 12 LCD keys that are the same size and shape as typical Stream Deck keys. There's a 2.75-inch LCD screen above the keys, which is divided into quadrants that are controlled by the two notched, clickable rotary knobs at the top. The Stream Deck is a true Stream Deck, so it has all the functionality of Elgato's platform, and can be easily programmed with the Stream Deck software. The keyboard also comes with a soft-touch plastic wrist rest, two USB cables, and a handful of other accessories in the box. You can read my full review of the Corsair Galleon 100 SD here. — Sarah

The Turtle Beach Atlas Air lives up to its name — this wireless, open-back headset is lightweight and airy in both comfort and sound. Although its all-plastic design didn't feel quite up to the $179.99 price point it debuted at, the comfort and audio quality was enough for us to recommend it — and now it's down to just $119.99 at Amazon for Black Friday.

The only wireless open-back gaming headset on the market is incredibly light and comfortable and sounds great. It has a detachable, flip-to-mute boom mic, dual-mode wireless connectivity, and gets about 50 hours of battery life.

The Atlas Air is a wireless, open-back headset, which means the sound isn't closed in. While this does mean that people around you can hear what you're listening to, there are several benefits to an open-back design — specifically, you don't get the same listening fatigue you get when listening to a closed-back headset, because the sound can escape instead of reverberating inside your head. For gamers, it also allows for a wider soundstage and a more immersive environment. As long as you don't work in close quarters, an open-back headset is a nice option if you don't want to commit to speakers.

The Atlas Air has a lightweight, plastic build, with a mesh suspension headband and floating earcups. It's extremely lightweight — just 10.61oz / 301g — and it basically feels like you're wearing nothing. It sports 40mm dynamic drivers with a frequency response range of 20 - 40,000 Hz, and it sounds surprisingly good: it has a nice, wide soundstage and a slightly bass-heavy sound profile, and it did especially well with picking up details in layered audio environments, such as cities and jungles. It's probably not the headset for those looking to gain advantage in shooting games — the directional sound is fine, but a closed-back headset will help you zero in on footsteps and gunshots. But for the less competitive games, this is a great option, especially if you find other headsets hard to wear for long periods of time. You can read my full review of the Atlas Air here. — Sarah

The Razer Naga V2 Pro is one of my favorite mice of all time, because I can never have enough buttons on a mouse. This wireless mouse is aimed at MMO / MOBA players, but it can actually be used by just about anyone thanks to the three swappable side plates it comes bundled with. Naturally, this kind of versatility doesn't come cheap, but right now you can grab the Naga V2 Pro for just $129.99 at Amazon — $50 off its MSRP of $179.99.

The Razer Naga V2 Pro sports a customizable magnetic side plate, offering 12-, 6-, and 2-button configurations, Razer's Hyperscroll Pro wheel, fully wireless connectivity, and its Focus Pro 30K Optical sensor.

The Naga V2 Pro comes with three interchangeable side plates with 12-, 6-, and 2-button configurations. It's not the lightest mouse on the market — it weighs 4.72oz / 134g, but lightness is not what most MMO players are looking for. Instead, they're looking for comfort, and the Naga V2 Pro is a very comfortable mouse, with a contoured, ergonomic right-handed shape and a rest for your ring finger. It sports Razer's Focus Pro 30K optical sensor, which has a maximum sensitivity of 30,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 750 IPS and can handle up to 70 G's of acceleration. It also has a customizable tilt wheel, which can be tuned in Razer's Synapse software.

I used this mouse for two years straight, until I recently replaced it with the Razer Naga V3 Pro — more because my Naga V2 Pro was starting to look a little worse for the wear, not because it wasn't still a fantastic mouse. You can read my full review of the Razer Naga V2 Pro here. — Sarah

The HyperX Cloud III wired gaming headset is one of the most comfortable headsets we've ever tested — it's almost exactly the same as the HyperX Cloud III S Wireless, just, well, wired. It has a premium build with a steel headband and curved aluminum forks, large over-ear earcups with leatherette-covered memory foam padding, and a leatherette-covered padded headband. It's sleek and understated, with a detachable boom microphone, and it's fairly lightweight at just 10.86oz / 308g. And it's currently on sale for $39 at Walmart — down $60.99 from its MSRP of $99.99.

The HyperX Cloud III is a wired gaming headset with a detachable microphone. It features 53mm drivers and virtual surround sound support.

The Cloud III wired gaming headset is basically the most comfortable headset we've tested in recent years. It's fairly adjustable, with earcups that tilt and are independently height-adjustable (they don't pivot, but the forks allow for some lateral movement and the headband is very flexible). The memory foam padding is thick and soft enough to wear comfortably over glasses, and the clamping force is practically perfect — enough that it won't fall off if you tilt your head back, but not much stronger than that. Add this into the weight and you have a headset that you can wear for hours and hours at a time without needing a break.

The headset sports HyperX's angled 53mm dynamic drivers, which have a frequency response range of 10 - 21,000 Hz — slightly outside the typical frequency response range of most gaming headsets, and nicely tuned to give you a neutral audio profile that still brings plenty of bass. This is the wired version, and it comes with an analog cable that can plug into a USB cable extension, which gives you plenty of length for when you're sitting at a PC while still being able to plug into any standard 3.5mm jack. It was already a good deal at its starting $100 price point, and at $39 it's absolutely worth it.

You can read my full review of the HyperX Cloud III wired gaming headset here. — Sarah

The quirky G3S case from Wokyis might be pushing the limits of practicality (not to mention copyright infringement), but it sure is cute and nostalgic. It’s a plastic shell that tips your Mac Mini (M6, M5 Pro, and M4 models) on its side and turns it into a tiny Power Mac G3 tower.

Whether you were a Mac fan in the late 90s or not, there’s a whole lot of nostalgia in this design. It’s available in four colors and is currently 50% off, taking it down to $19.99 at Amazon.

This ABS plastic Mac Mini case is pure nostalgia and not all that practical, but there are benefits to tipping Apple’s smallest Mac up on its side.

Aside from the throwback 90s looks, tipping the Mac Mini on its side like this actually lets you press the power button without lifting up the mini PC. Plus, if your desk space is cramped, putting the system on its side will free up some room. -- Matt Safford

If you're in the market for a current-gen RTX 50-series card that won't set you back thousands of dollars, then this might be the deal for you. Newegg is selling the cheapest RTX 5060 you can buy right now at $439.99, an $80 saving. While that's a far cry from the MSRP of $299, GPUs are very expensive these days, so this is about as good as it gets for 1080p gaming.

Get an RTX 5060 with 8GB of GDDR7 VRAM, clock speeds of 2550 MHz, 3840 CUDA cores, and a free GPU holder.

At 1080p, the RTX 5060 can put out more than 60 fps, making it perfect for entry-level gaming. It also supports Nvidia's DLSS technologies, so you can squeeze out more frames or even try your hand at 1440p.

This specific version of the RTX 5060 is Zotac's AMP series, with core clocks of 2550 MHz, with the same speed listed for its boost clocks. It has 3840 CUDA cores, and 8GB of GDDR7 VRAM with a 128-bit memory interface. While this won't blow titles out of the water at 4K, this is budget gaming performance at a time when GPUs are becoming increasingly more expensive. - Stephen Warwick

Buying a PC on Black Friday doesn't have to mean spending the Earth. If you want a budget build, this Intel Core i7 14700F rig from Cyberpower is a fantastic cheap option for 1080p gaming. With an RTX 5060 Ti 8GB, this should be brilliant for entry-level gaming and could even be pushed to 1440p with Nvidia's DLSS technology.

The CyberPower Gamer Xtreme prebuilt PC offers a 20-Core Intel i7 14700F CPU, RTX 5060 Ti GPU, 16GB of DDR5 memory, and 1 TB of storage, wrapped up in a white case, and flush with glowing RGB fans.

As you can see from our testing data, in our 19-game testing suite, the RTX 5060 Ti 8GB is good for average frame rates of 72 fps. This drops to around 46 at 1440p without any help from frame generation.

The CPU in this build is Intel's i7 14700F with 20 cores and 28 threads, boasting boost clocks of up to 5.4 GHz- a great processor for productivity and gaming.

Aside from the potent 20-core CPU and GPU for 1080, you also get 16GB of DDR5 RAM and a 1TB SSD. Windows 11 Home comes as standard, and the motherboard supports Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.3. There are also ports aplenty. - Stephen Warwick

Samsung's P9 Express microSDXC is one of the top storage solutions for Nintendo Switch 2. With transfer speeds of up to 800 MB/s and similar sequential read speeds, this is a speedy storage solution for your handheld.

The Switch 2 ships with 256GB of internal storage as standard, so a 512GB expansion will triple that capacity for storing games and files. While not quite its lowest-ever price, there's a great deal on this card, 38% off at Amazon, now just $92.99.

The Samsung P9 is a microSD Express card that offers great performance and reliability for its price. The 512GB model is currently priced at its original MSRP of $99.99.

The P9 Express comes with Dynamic Thermal Guard technology to stop your card from overheating while in use for smoother gameplay. It also has a three-year warranty and can be used with microSD UHS-I devices such as tablets and drones, too.

The 256GB model is also on sale, an arguably better value. At 44% off, it's less than half the price of the 512GB model. In theory, buying two would get you the same amount of storage for $89, provided you don't mind swapping cards around.

The Samsung P9 is a microSD Express card that offers great performance and reliability for its price. The 256GB model is currently priced at its original MSRP of $44.99.

With SSD and flash storage prices through the roof thanks to AI, this is a solid deal on a great Nintendo Switch 2 card. - Stephen Warwick

I use the Gateron Oil King Ghost Pro switches on my own keyboard, and they're a go-to linear switch for a good reason. The heavier 50gf operating force is heavier than a standard Red-style switch, leading to a deep sound and more pronounced feedback while typing, particularly if you're a heavy typer.

The Oil King Ghost Pro switches are linear key switches for a mechanical keyboard with a 50gf operating force.

These switches are an upgraded version of standard Oil Kings, with the new Ghost name noting the passthrough channel for lighting. The switches themselves are the same, and they come factory lubricated, so they sound great out of the box. You can use the switches with any standard 3-pin or 5-pin PCB — Jake Roach

This hefty Lenovo Legion gaming laptop is the first RTX 5090-powered laptop we've seen under $4,000. This is a huge spec with a 240Hz OLED display, 24GB VRAM GPU, a massive 24-core Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX CPU, 32GB of DDR5 RAM, and a 1TB SSD.

The 16-inch Lenovo Legion Pro 7i gaming laptop comes with an Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus CPU, RTX 5090 (175W TGP) GPU, 32GB of DDR5 memory, and 1TB of storage. The OLED display offers a 240Hz refresh rate and a 2560 x 1600 resolution.

With its 24 cores and performance core boost clocks of up to 5.5 GHz, this is a fantastic mobile CPU for both work and play. Combined with the laptop RTX 5090, the best laptop GPU on the market, this will make light work of any title you can throw at it in the 2560 x 1200 resolution. That stunning OLED will really make games pop, too.

Also offers 1x Thunderbolt 4 port (USB-C), 1x 3.2 Gen 2 (USB-C), 1x USB 3.2 Gen 2 (USB-A), 2x USB 3.2 Gen 1 (USB-A), a 3.5mm headphone jack, 1x HDMI 2.1 port, and a 2.5 Gbps Ethernet jack, as well as Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4. While we haven't reviewed this specific spec, in our Lenovo Legion Pro 7i Gen 10 review, the laptop scored very well thanks to its exceptional OLED screen, aluminum chassis, and sharp webcam. - Stephen Warwick

Earlier this week, we highlighted a great deal on Apple's MacBook Neo, which is $100 off and back to its original launch price of $599. This is also better than the previous $50 discount to $649, so if you missed out the first time, this deal is now better! The $599 price gets you 256GB of storage and 8GB of RAM, and is available in all four of Apple's vibrant colors.

You can also snag the 512GB version for $699, a $100 discount.

Apple's base MacBook Neo has an A18 Pro chip, 256GB of storage, and 8GB of RAM. A solid alternative with a more powerful SoC.

The A18 Pro chip in the MacBook Neo is solid for single-core productivity performance excelling in single-core performance, though the 8GB can be difficult for serious multitasking. For people working on basic tasks, this is going to be sufficient.There have been a handful of other deals on the Neo so far this week. We saw the base model drop to $599 (in citrus only) at one point, while the upgraded 512GB model with Touch ID dropped to $699 (in blush) at another. It's possible we'll see more color-specific price drops, but it's not a guarantee, and $649 isn't bad given the RAM situation. — Andrew E. Freedman

In what might be one of the best gaming PC deals we've seen so far, this HyperX OMEN desktop at Best Buy, featuring Intel's Core Ultra 7 270K Plus and RTX 5080 GPU, is now just $2,699. The graphics card in this build alone currently retails for around $1,700, making this a really good value build.

Get an RTX 5080 PC with Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus, 16GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD, with plenty of space to upgrade. Also features Wi-Fi 7.

The star of the show here is the RTX 5080, a fully-fledged 4K GPU that will take care of any title you want to play at high resolutions and settings. That's complemented by the Intel Core Ultra 7 270K, a much-improved Intel gaming CPU released not too long ago. With 24 cores, it performs extremely well in productivity tasks as well as gaming. While it can't quite match the X3D SKUs of AMD for gaming performance, it is still a very strong desktop CPU.

The supporting cast of the build is perhaps the only compromise. The 1TB SSD is fine to get you started, but 16GB of RAM is a little less than we'd like in a build of this caliber. Still, this is such a cheap build for an RTX 5080 that it will be worth the trade-off for some. Of course, if you already have some DDR5 RAM lying around, you could swap that in, or you could spend some of that $1,700 saving on an upgrade.

The build supports up to 128GB of memory, with 4 DIMM slots for future expansion. It also has two further SSD slots, as well as Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0, thanks to the Intel Z890 motherboard inside.

This build will not be around for long, so move fast if you want to grab one. - Stephen Warwick

Whether you need to upgrade your boot drive or you’re attempting to rescue the laptop or gaming PC of a friend or family member, an SSD cloner can make a scary, potentially tedious job surprisingly easy. I know because I bought this cloner a couple of years ago (when it cost about $15 more) and moved someone’s existing OS from an extremely cramped 128GB drive onto a faster 512GB drive in less than half an hour. And now Rosewill’s SSD cloner is on sale for its lowest-ever price at Amazon.

With support for NVMe M.2 SSDs and offline cloning, this handy device makes it simple to move your files or OS from one drive to another. And with a 20 Gbps USB-C interface, it's also speedy in your OS of choice if you want to use software to clone or move your data between drives.

Keep in mind this device only supports M Key PCIe / NVMe drives, so it won’t work with SATA M.2 drives. But it can work both as a standalone drive or with software if you need to, say, resize the partition. The Rosewill cloner is also handy for checking the contents of M.2 drives you may have lying around. But if that's all you need, you can get a good tool-free enclosure for less than $20. -- Matt Safford

Hello and welcome to day two of our Black Friday coverage, Stephen here to see you through the early hours of the morning!

#10376. Google Pixel held its ground in the US despite a middling Pixel 11 launch

The latest quarterly data for the US smartphone market reveals that Google Pixel is holding its ground despite the overall market faltering, and the other two major Android brands struggling.

The top smartphone brands in the United States include Apple, Samsung, Motorola, and Google Pixel in that order. Apple continues to absolutely dominate at a whopping 57% market share in Q3 2026, up from 50% during the same period last year.

Samsung came in at 25%, up 1% from last year (likely driven by a very successful Fold 8 launch during Q3), while Motorola shrank from 12% to 8%.

Google Pixel made up 6%, down 1% from Q3 2025, Counterpoint Research shows. Q3 is important for Google as it includes the company’s new August release window for new flagships. It’s not surprising that Google dropped a percentage point year-over-year, as the company’s Pixel 11 launch was not particularly exciting, especially as prices rose over the previous generation. If anything, only dropping 1% must be pretty encouraging given the overall market conditions and RAMageddon of it all.

Something to note – Google Pixel is technically growing this year compared to last. Just out of view on this latest update, Q2 2026 saw Google’s share up 1% year-over-year, and Q1 was also up compared to the same period in 2025. Counterpoint previously mentioned that the Pixel brand “remains aggressive in postpaid” carriers, but notes that Pixel 11 shipments were “weaker YoY.”

Serious performance for a brilliant price

There's an unmissable deal on an RTX 5080 gaming PC over at HP right now. The company has slashed $1,700 off one of its gaming-focused HyperX Omen 35L rigs, a machine fitted with an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 for just $2,699.99 right now.

That's an incredible price when you consider how much the RTX 5080 currently costs outright. Of what little stock there is, the cheapest card you can buy is $1,999, with high-end cards costing over $3,000. That's more than you'd be paying for this entire gaming PC combined.

No doubt about it, this is a high-spec rig from a premium gaming brand, but without the premium price tag. This will deliver 4K gaming with high frame rates on the best graphics presets, supported by Nvidia DLSS and multi-frame generation for the most seriously intensive games if you spot any performance drops.

Get an RTX 5080 PC from HP's HyperX gaming brand with Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus, 16GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD, with plenty of space to upgrade. Also features Wi-Fi 7.

The GPU is the focal point of this build, and the one that gives it the performance you'll need for high-end gaming. The Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 is the second most powerful consumer GPU available from this current generation, as our GPU benchmarks will confirm. As a result, you'll be getting a GPU with 10,752 CUDA cores and 16GB of GDDR7 VRAM.

Only the RTX 5090 can best it on specs, and as a result, you'll be able to cleanly play at 4K. The Bench charts below confirm that the RTX 5080 has very few rivals, sitting near the top of the GPU food chain.

Intel CPUs might not be as popular for gaming these days, but the Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus CPU used here isn't a compromise. Far from it: our 270K Plus review confirms that, especially for productivity, you're getting a serious performer and a great all-rounder. It didn't give the best impression for gaming initially but, after subsequent retesting and analysis for our CPU benchmarks, we've seen that the 270K Plus is only slightly behind its last-gen flagship (and still very popular) i9-14900K, with even better scoring for productivity users.

A dominant trio, and for gamers, you're getting a 1TB SSD offering Gen 4 speeds, so you'll be able to get at least one or two of the biggest games installed alongside Windows. The only compromise, really, is the RAM. 16GB of DDR5 memory is included here, rated for speeds of 5,600 MT/s. That's a disappointment but, at this price, you've still got room for maneuver if you decide to upgrade to 32GB or 64GB (or higher) later. You're also getting a rig with Wi-Fi 7 support, along with 2.5 Gb Ethernet for high-speed wired connections, so you won't see any slowdowns while you're gaming online.

This is a build that will last for years and will let you play at the highest resolutions doing it, but don't expect this deal to be around for long. Garmin and Bark are competing for your money this year, and these sales make it easy to get something fun that’ll keep your kids safe and in touch.

Many parents struggle with the idea of getting a smartphone for their kids. If you want your kids to stay in touch but not have access to all the garbage on the internet, a smartwatch is the best alternative. I’ve tested a lot of kids’ smartwatches over the years, and I can easily recommend the two in the picture above: the Bark Watch and the Garmin Bounce 2.

The least expensive Garmin Bounce 2 is the blue color in the photo I took above, which my son loved.

Choosing between the two is easy enough. Garmin’s watch is the least complicated and comes in a slightly more durable case with fun colors. Bark charges $15 per month for its plan, which includes a Bark App subscription for the whole family. I also use the Bark App on my son’s phone, which helps me monitor his usage and make sure he’s safe online. The extra $5 per month adds up, but it’s absolutely worth it if you want to add the Bark App to another phone or tablet.

The Bark Watch is fine enough for younger kids, but the design and lack of games feel more like an “older kids’ watch” to me, and my 12-year-old son agrees. Either way you go, these are fantastic choices that you’ll be happy with, especially with a nice little deal.
